newsitem.title: UK: Two-tier CGT tax for UK "deeply flawed"-- IFS.
newsitem.headline: Two-tier CGT tax for UK "deeply flawed"-- IFS.

text.p: The Institute for Fiscal Studies said a two-tier capital gains tax (CGT) -- a possibility raised in the new Labour government's election manifesto -- was deeply flawed and would raise little revenue.
Labour has said it would consider levying a higher rate of CGT where assets have been held for only a short time, the intention being to encourage investors to hold assets long-term.
"This proposal is deeply flawed at both the conceptual and the pragmatic levels," the IFS said in its so-called Green Budget, in which it details its forecasts for the forthcoming budget.
A two-tier CGT would have almost no impact on shareholders' behaviour as hardly any shareholders in Britain pay the tax.
Pension funds are exempt, as are insurance companies in relation to their pension business, while individuals can shelter gains in personal equity plans and make use of annual exemptions.

Only 85,000 taxpayers paid CGT in 1994/95, the latest year for which figures are available, and the tax raised only 800 million stg. By contrast, 25 million people paid income tax and the revenue raised that year totalled 63 billion stg.

"Tapering the rate of capital gains tax would add considerably to the complexity of an already complex tax and would be more good news for the tax planning industry," the IFS said. "But it could not be expected to make any significant difference to the environment for long-term investment."
